Chapter 6  ·  Probabilistic Classification

Probabilistic Classification
& Bayes Decision Theory

From uncertain observations to optimal predictions: how probability transforms classification into principled risk minimization.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why overlapping class distributions make deterministic classification impossible and motivate a probabilistic approach.
  • State Bayes' theorem and apply it to convert class-conditional probabilities and priors into posterior probabilities.
  • Define prior, class-conditional, and posterior probabilities and identify each in a concrete classification problem.
  • Define a loss function, distinguish symmetric from asymmetric loss, and evaluate expected loss for a binary decision.
  • Define statistical risk as expected loss and derive the Bayes decision rule as its minimizer.
  • Extend the discrete Bayes classifier to continuous feature spaces using probability density functions.
  • Identify when the optimal decision boundary is not the maximum-posterior boundary and adjust for asymmetric loss.
  • Compute the Bayes risk and interpret it as the irreducible error floor of any classifier.

6.1 Why Probabilistic Classification?

Every classifier we have studied so far — the perceptron, support vector machines — has been built around the idea of finding a decision boundary: a geometric surface that cleanly separates the positive class from the negative class. These methods are powerful, but they rest on an implicit assumption that the classes are, at least in principle, separable. They treat the label of each training point as a ground truth, and they try to reproduce that labeling with a function of the features.

Real data rarely cooperates. In many of the most important classification problems — medical diagnosis, spam detection, fraud detection, speech recognition — the mapping from features to labels is inherently stochastic. Two people with identical symptoms may have or not have a disease. Two emails with identical word counts may or may not be spam. The label is not a deterministic function of the observed features; it is a random variable. Any classifier that pretends otherwise is doomed to misclassify some fraction of examples no matter how sophisticated it becomes, because the ground truth itself is probabilistic.

This chapter introduces a new family of classifiers that embrace this uncertainty. Instead of learning a boundary, we will learn a model of the probability distribution of the data, and then use that model to make principled decisions. The tools we need are Bayes' theorem, the concept of expected loss, and the notion of statistical risk — all of which we will develop carefully here and use throughout the rest of the course.

6.1.1 Overlapping Distributions and Irreducible Uncertainty

Consider a classic example. Suppose we want to build a classifier that takes a single feature — an adult's height — and predicts their sex. We have training data: heights of men and heights of women. If we plot the histogram of those heights, we see two bell-shaped curves with substantial overlap. A height of 5 feet 5 inches (approximately 165 cm) is common among both men and women; there is no way to be certain about the correct label for a test point at this value.

Definition · Irreducible Error

Let $X \in \mathcal{X}$ be a feature vector and $Y \in \{+1, -1\}$ a class label, with joint distribution $P(X, Y)$. The irreducible error (or Bayes error rate) is $$R^* = \mathbb{E}_{X}\bigl[1 - \max_{y \in \{+1,-1\}} P(Y = y \mid X)\bigr],$$ where the expectation is over the marginal distribution of $X$. No classifier can achieve an error rate below $R^*$.

The irreducible error is the price we pay for having overlapping class-conditional distributions. Even the best possible classifier — one with perfect knowledge of every relevant probability — cannot avoid misclassifying the points that sit deep inside the overlap region. For the height example, a 5'5" individual is classified as "female" by any reasonable classifier, but roughly 45% of the time that prediction will be wrong. That 45% is irreducible; it is a property of the data-generating process, not of our algorithm.

Figure 6.1. Class-conditional height distributions for women (blue, $\mu \approx 5'4''$, $\sigma \approx 0.28'$) and men (gold, $\mu \approx 5'11''$, $\sigma \approx 0.30'$). The dashed red line marks the test point at 5'5". In the region of overlap, neither class has an overwhelming advantage; classifying the red test point as "female" gives roughly a 55% chance of correctness — the remaining 45% is irreducible error for a classifier using only height.

6.1.2 From Labels to Class Probabilities

The key insight motivating this chapter is that the right output of a classifier is not necessarily a hard label but a probability. Given a test point $\mathbf{x}$, the ideal classifier computes $P(Y = +1 \mid X = \mathbf{x})$ — the probability that the true label is positive — and then makes a decision based on that probability and on the consequences of each type of error. This probability-first view has several advantages over the hard-boundary view.

  • Uncertainty quantification: A doctor who knows that a patient has a 36% probability of cancer can make a much more nuanced treatment decision than one who receives only a binary "cancer / no cancer" prediction.
  • Loss-sensitivity: When the consequences of different types of errors are unequal — as in medical diagnosis or fraud detection — the hard-boundary view has no natural mechanism to incorporate this. Probabilistic outputs, combined with a loss function, provide a principled way to do so.
  • Calibration: A model whose probability estimates accurately reflect true frequencies is called calibrated. Calibration is a measurable, desirable property that makes sense only in the probabilistic framework.
Data Science Application · Probabilistic Outputs in Production ML

In industry, most deployed classifiers output probability scores rather than hard labels. A spam filter that outputs $P(\text{spam} \mid \text{email}) = 0.92$ lets the system administrator set a threshold appropriate for their users' tolerance for false positives and false negatives. A logistic regression model, a random forest's class-fraction outputs, and the softmax layer of a neural network all produce probabilistic outputs of this form. The framework developed in this chapter — specifically the concepts of posterior probability and risk minimization — provides the theoretical foundation for every such system.

6.2 Bayes' Theorem and the Posterior

The central computational challenge of probabilistic classification is a reversal problem. What we can often measure or estimate from training data is the probability distribution of features within each class: "Given that this patient has cancer, how likely is it that they work in mining?" What we need for classification is the reverse: "Given that this person works in mining, how likely is it that they have cancer?" Bayes' theorem is precisely the mathematical tool that performs this reversal.

6.2.1 Prior, Class-Conditional, and Posterior

We work with a binary label $Y \in \{+1, -1\}$ and a discrete feature $X$ taking values in some finite set $\mathcal{X}$. The generalization to continuous features is taken up in Section 6.5.

Definition · Key Probability Quantities

Given random variables $X$ (features) and $Y$ (class label), define:

  • Prior probability: $P(Y = y)$ for $y \in \{+1, -1\}$ — the marginal probability of each class, before observing any features.
  • Class-conditional probability: $P(X = x \mid Y = y)$ — the probability of observing feature value $x$ given that the class is $y$. This is what training data within each class directly estimates.
  • Evidence (marginal): $P(X = x) = \sum_{y} P(X = x \mid Y = y)\, P(Y = y)$ — the overall probability of observing feature $x$, summed over all classes.
  • Posterior probability: $P(Y = y \mid X = x)$ — the probability of class $y$ given the observed feature $x$. This is the quantity we use for classification.

Theorem · Bayes' Theorem (Classification Form)

For any feature value $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and class label $y \in \{+1,-1\}$, provided $P(X = x) > 0$:

$$\boxed{P(Y = y \mid X = x) = \frac{P(X = x \mid Y = y)\, P(Y = y)}{P(X = x)}}$$

where $P(X = x) = \sum_{y' \in \{+1,-1\}} P(X = x \mid Y = y')\, P(Y = y')$.

Proof

By the definition of conditional probability, $$P(Y = y \mid X = x) = \frac{P(X = x,\, Y = y)}{P(X = x)}.$$ Applying the chain rule of probability to the numerator: $P(X = x, Y = y) = P(X = x \mid Y = y)\, P(Y = y)$. Substituting and expanding the denominator by the law of total probability: $$P(X = x) = \sum_{y'} P(X = x \mid Y = y')\, P(Y = y').$$ Combining these three steps yields Bayes' theorem. □

Intuition · What Bayes' Theorem Actually Does

Think of the prior $P(Y=y)$ as your belief about class membership before seeing any data about an individual. The class-conditional $P(X=x \mid Y=y)$ tells you how "characteristic" a particular feature value is of each class. Bayes' theorem multiplies these together — your prior belief scaled by how well the evidence fits each class — and then normalizes the result to sum to one across all classes. The denominator $P(X=x)$ is just the normalization constant; it ensures the posterior is a valid probability distribution. For classification, this normalization constant is the same for all classes and therefore cancels when comparing posteriors — which is why we often skip computing it (see Section 6.5).

6.2.2 The Cancer Diagnosis Example

Let us work through a concrete example that will anchor the ideas throughout this chapter. Suppose we want to diagnose whether a patient has cancer ($Y = +1$) or does not ($Y = -1$), using a single feature: their occupation $X \in \{\text{miner},\, \text{farmer},\, \text{other}\}$. This is a deliberately crude model — no reasonable physician would diagnose cancer this way — but it serves to illustrate the mathematics cleanly.

We are given the following data:

Occupation $X$$P(X \mid Y=+1)$ (Cancer)$P(X \mid Y=-1)$ (No Cancer)
Miner0.200.01
Farmer0.500.10
Other0.300.89

We also know the prior probabilities: $P(Y=+1) = 0.10$ (10% of the population has cancer) and $P(Y=-1) = 0.90$. Notice that each column of the table sums to 1: these are proper probability mass functions for occupation, conditioned on the diagnosis.

6.2.3 Normalizing by the Evidence

Before we can compute the posterior, we need the marginal probability of each occupation — the denominator in Bayes' theorem. For a farmer:

$$P(X = \text{farmer}) = P(X=\text{farmer} \mid Y=+1)\, P(Y=+1) + P(X=\text{farmer} \mid Y=-1)\, P(Y=-1)$$ $$= 0.50 \times 0.10 + 0.10 \times 0.90 = 0.05 + 0.09 = 0.14.$$

That is, 14% of the overall population are farmers. Now Bayes' theorem gives us the posterior probability of cancer given the patient is a farmer:

Posterior via Bayes
$$P(Y=+1 \mid X=\text{farmer}) = \frac{P(X=\text{farmer} \mid Y=+1)\, P(Y=+1)}{P(X=\text{farmer})} = \frac{0.05}{0.14} \approx 0.357$$

This is a crucial result. A naive reading of the class-conditional table suggests that farmers are strongly associated with cancer (50% of cancer patients are farmers, vs.\ only 10% of healthy patients). But that naive reading completely ignores the prior: cancer is rare. Applying Bayes' theorem, we find that only about 36% of farmers have cancer. The prior "dilutes" the class-conditional evidence.

Example · Full Posterior Computation for All Occupations

Let us compute the posteriors for all three occupations systematically.

Step 1: Compute $P(X=x)$ for each $x$.

  • $P(\text{miner}) = 0.20 \times 0.10 + 0.01 \times 0.90 = 0.020 + 0.009 = 0.029$
  • $P(\text{farmer}) = 0.50 \times 0.10 + 0.10 \times 0.90 = 0.050 + 0.090 = 0.140$
  • $P(\text{other}) = 0.30 \times 0.10 + 0.89 \times 0.90 = 0.030 + 0.801 = 0.831$

Check: $0.029 + 0.140 + 0.831 = 1.000.$ ✓

Step 2: Apply Bayes' theorem.

  • $P(Y{=}+1 \mid \text{miner}) = 0.020 / 0.029 \approx 0.690$
  • $P(Y{=}+1 \mid \text{farmer}) = 0.050 / 0.140 \approx 0.357$
  • $P(Y{=}+1 \mid \text{other}) = 0.030 / 0.831 \approx 0.036$

Interpretation: Miners have a 69% posterior probability of cancer — far higher than the 10% base rate — while "other" occupations have only a 3.6% chance. Despite half of all cancer patients being farmers, a given farmer has only a 36% chance of having cancer, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick people.

Figure 6.2. Left panel: the class-conditional probabilities $P(\text{occupation} \mid \text{diagnosis})$ as given in the data — these can be misleading without accounting for the prior. Right panel: the posterior probabilities $P(\text{diagnosis} \mid \text{occupation})$ after applying Bayes' theorem with prior $P(Y=+1)=0.10$. Notice how the high class-conditional probability for farmers (50%) is drastically reduced in the posterior (36%) once the 10% base rate is accounted for. Red = cancer; blue = no cancer.
Warning · The Base Rate Fallacy

The most common mistake in probabilistic reasoning is to read class-conditional probabilities as if they were posteriors. Because 50% of cancer patients are farmers, a student might conclude "farmers probably have cancer." This is wrong: it ignores the prior $P(Y=+1) = 0.10$. The correct posterior for a farmer is only 36%. Whenever you are handed probabilities of the form $P(\text{feature} \mid \text{class})$, remember that Bayes' theorem is needed before you can make a classification decision. This error has been called the base rate fallacy or prosecutor's fallacy in the statistics literature.

6.3 Loss Functions

Knowing that a farmer has a 36% chance of cancer does not by itself tell us what to do. Should we diagnose cancer, or not? The answer depends on the consequences of each possible decision. If diagnosing cancer triggers a biopsy, the cost of a false positive (unnecessary biopsy) might be modest. If it triggers immediate surgery, the cost is much higher. If failing to diagnose cancer means the patient goes home and an early-stage tumor goes untreated, the cost of a false negative could be catastrophic. Probability alone is not enough; we need a way to quantify the badness of different kinds of errors. This is the role of the loss function.

6.3.1 Defining and Interpreting Loss

Definition · Loss Function

A loss function $L : \{+1,-1\} \times \{+1,-1\} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ maps a predicted label $\hat{y}$ and a true label $y$ to a non-negative real number $L(\hat{y}, y)$ measuring the cost of predicting $\hat{y}$ when the truth is $y$. A loss function must satisfy:

  • Non-negativity: $L(\hat{y}, y) \geq 0$ for all $\hat{y}, y$.
  • Zero correct-prediction loss: $L(y, y) = 0$ for all $y$ (correct predictions incur no loss).
The four entries of $L$ for a binary classifier are: $$\begin{array}{c|cc} L(\hat{y}, y) & y = +1 & y = -1 \\ \hline \hat{y}=+1 & 0 & L_{\text{fp}} \\ \hat{y}=-1 & L_{\text{fn}} & 0 \end{array}$$ where $L_{\text{fp}} > 0$ is the false-positive loss and $L_{\text{fn}} > 0$ is the false-negative loss.

6.3.2 Symmetric vs. Asymmetric Loss

If $L_{\text{fp}} = L_{\text{fn}}$, the loss function is symmetric: both types of errors are equally bad. If $L_{\text{fp}} \neq L_{\text{fn}}$, it is asymmetric. Asymmetric losses are the norm in most real-world applications.

For the cancer example, suppose we set $L_{\text{fp}} = 1$ (send patient for an unnecessary biopsy — inconvenient but not dangerous) and $L_{\text{fn}} = 5$ (send patient home with undiagnosed cancer — potentially fatal). With these numbers, a false negative is five times worse than a false positive.

Figure 6.3. Loss matrices for binary classification. Left: the 0–1 loss function, where every mistake costs exactly 1 and every correct prediction costs 0. Right: an asymmetric loss for cancer diagnosis, where a false negative (predicting "no cancer" when the patient has cancer) is penalized with $L_{\text{fn}} = 5$, five times the false-positive penalty $L_{\text{fp}} = 1$. The loss values are color-coded: white = 0 (correct), yellow-red = positive loss (incorrect).
Example · Expected Loss for the Farmer

Recall that $P(Y=+1 \mid X=\text{farmer}) \approx 0.357$ and $P(Y=-1 \mid X=\text{farmer}) \approx 0.643$. With $L_{\text{fp}}=1$ and $L_{\text{fn}}=5$:

Expected loss if we predict cancer ($\hat{y} = +1$): $$\mathbb{E}[L \mid \hat{y}=+1,\, X=\text{farmer}] = L_{\text{fp}} \cdot P(Y=-1 \mid \text{farmer}) = 1 \times 0.643 = 0.643.$$ This is the expected cost of making this positive prediction: most farmers don't have cancer, so we'll be wrong 64% of the time and pay $L_{\text{fp}}=1$ each time.

Expected loss if we predict no cancer ($\hat{y} = -1$): $$\mathbb{E}[L \mid \hat{y}=-1,\, X=\text{farmer}] = L_{\text{fn}} \cdot P(Y=+1 \mid \text{farmer}) = 5 \times 0.357 = 1.785.$$

Decision: Since $0.643 < 1.785$, we minimize expected loss by predicting cancer for farmers, even though the posterior probability of cancer is only 36%. The asymmetric loss overrides what a simple "predict the majority class" rule would give us.

Intuition · Why Asymmetric Loss Shifts the Threshold

Under symmetric 0–1 loss, we predict the class with the higher posterior probability — in this case "no cancer" (64% posterior) would win. But asymmetric loss changes the comparison. Multiplying the cancer posterior by $L_{\text{fn}}=5$ and the no-cancer posterior by $L_{\text{fp}}=1$, we effectively ask: "Which mistake is more expensive in expectation?" When a false negative is five times costlier than a false positive, we are willing to predict cancer even when it is the less probable outcome. The threshold at which we switch from "predict no cancer" to "predict cancer" shifts from $p=0.5$ (for 0–1 loss) down to $p = L_{\text{fp}}/(L_{\text{fp}} + L_{\text{fn}}) = 1/6 \approx 0.167$ for our asymmetric loss.

6.3.3 The 0–1 Loss Function

The most commonly used loss function is also the simplest: assign a loss of 1 to every mistake and 0 to every correct prediction, regardless of the direction of the error.

Definition · 0–1 Loss Function

The 0–1 loss function is defined by $$L_{01}(\hat{y}, y) = \mathbf{1}[\hat{y} \neq y] = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \hat{y} = y \\ 1 & \text{if } \hat{y} \neq y \end{cases}$$ for all $\hat{y}, y \in \{+1, -1\}$. Under this loss, the expected loss equals the probability of misclassification: $$\mathbb{E}[L_{01}(\hat{y}, Y)] = P(\hat{y} \neq Y).$$ The 0–1 loss is symmetric: $L_{\text{fp}} = L_{\text{fn}} = 1$.

Unless told otherwise, we use 0–1 loss as the default. Under 0–1 loss, the optimal prediction at any test point is simply the class with the highest posterior probability — a result we prove formally in Section 6.4.

💡
Connection to spam filtering: A real-world spam filter does not use 0–1 loss. Missing an important email (false negative: marking a real email as spam) is much worse than letting one piece of spam through (false positive). Asymmetric loss is therefore the right framework for setting the classification threshold in any deployed email filter.

6.4 Statistical Risk and the Bayes Decision Rule

We now have all the ingredients to formalize what it means to build an optimal classifier. We have a model of the data distribution (via class-conditional probabilities and a prior), and we have a loss function encoding the cost of different errors. What we want is a systematic procedure for constructing the best possible classifier given this information. The key concept is risk, and the key result is the Bayes decision rule.

6.4.1 Risk as Expected Loss

Definition · Decision Rule and Risk

A decision rule (or classifier) is a function $r : \mathcal{X} \to \{+1, -1\}$ mapping feature vectors to predicted labels.

The risk of a decision rule $r$ with respect to a loss function $L$ and joint distribution $P(X, Y)$ is the expected loss: $$R(r) = \mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)}[L(r(X),\, Y)] = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \sum_{y \in \{+1,-1\}} L(r(x),\, y)\, P(X=x,\, Y=y).$$ Note that $R(r)$ is a functional — a function whose argument is itself a function ($r$).

📌
Memorize this: Risk = Expected Loss. This single equation is one of the most important in statistical machine learning. Every classical learning algorithm can be understood as choosing a decision rule (or parameters of a model) to minimize some form of risk.

We can expand the double sum in the risk expression in a way that makes the role of the posteriors explicit. Using Bayes' theorem to rewrite $P(X=x, Y=y) = P(Y=y \mid X=x) P(X=x)$:

$$R(r) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \left[ \sum_{y \in \{+1,-1\}} L(r(x),\, y)\, P(Y=y \mid X=x) \right] P(X=x).$$

The inner sum is the conditional risk at the specific point $x$ — the expected loss given that we observe feature value $x$. To minimize the overall risk, it is sufficient to minimize this inner sum at every $x$ independently.

6.4.2 Deriving the Bayes-Optimal Classifier

Theorem · Bayes Decision Rule

Let $L$ be a loss function with $L(y,y)=0$ and $L(\hat{y},y)>0$ whenever $\hat{y}\neq y$. The decision rule that minimizes the risk $R(r)$ is: $$r^*(x) = \underset{y' \in \{+1,-1\}}{\operatorname*{arg\,min}}\; \sum_{y} L(y', y)\, P(Y=y \mid X=x).$$ Equivalently, $r^*$ predicts class $+1$ at point $x$ if and only if $$L_{\text{fn}} \cdot P(Y=+1 \mid X=x) > L_{\text{fp}} \cdot P(Y=-1 \mid X=x).$$ This rule is called the Bayes decision rule or Bayes classifier, and its risk $R^* = R(r^*)$ is the Bayes risk.

Proof

Since $R(r) = \sum_x [\cdots] P(X=x)$ and $P(X=x) \geq 0$ for all $x$, minimizing $R(r)$ is equivalent to minimizing the conditional risk at each $x$ independently. At a fixed $x$, the decision rule chooses either $r(x)=+1$ or $r(x)=-1$.

Conditional risk if $r(x) = +1$: $$\Delta_{+1}(x) = L(+1,+1)\, P(Y=+1 \mid x) + L(+1,-1)\, P(Y=-1 \mid x) = L_{\text{fp}}\, P(Y=-1 \mid x).$$ (The first term vanishes because $L(+1,+1) = 0$.)

Conditional risk if $r(x) = -1$: $$\Delta_{-1}(x) = L(-1,+1)\, P(Y=+1 \mid x) + L(-1,-1)\, P(Y=-1 \mid x) = L_{\text{fn}}\, P(Y=+1 \mid x).$$

We choose $r^*(x) = +1$ when $\Delta_{+1}(x) < \Delta_{-1}(x)$, i.e., when $L_{\text{fp}}\, P(Y=-1 \mid x) < L_{\text{fn}}\, P(Y=+1 \mid x)$, which rearranges to the stated condition. Ties can be broken arbitrarily. □

A particularly clean form of the Bayes rule emerges when we use 0–1 loss ($L_{\text{fp}} = L_{\text{fn}} = 1$): the condition $L_{\text{fn}} \cdot P(Y=+1 \mid x) > L_{\text{fp}} \cdot P(Y=-1 \mid x)$ reduces to simply $P(Y=+1 \mid x) > P(Y=-1 \mid x)$. That is, under symmetric loss, predict the class with the highest posterior probability.

Bayes Decision Rule
$$r^*(x) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } L_{\mathrm{fn}}\cdot P(Y=+1\mid X=x) > L_{\mathrm{fp}}\cdot P(Y=-1\mid X=x) \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Figure 6.5. Expected loss as a function of the posterior cancer probability $p = P(Y=+1 \mid X=x)$, for $L_{\text{fn}}=5$, $L_{\text{fp}}=1$. The red curve is the expected loss of predicting "cancer"; the blue curve is the expected loss of predicting "no cancer." The gold dashed line marks the optimal threshold $p^* = L_{\text{fp}}/(L_{\text{fp}} + L_{\text{fn}}) = 1/6 \approx 0.167$: below this threshold predict "no cancer," above it predict "cancer." The purple dotted line marks the farmer's posterior ($p \approx 0.36$), which lies above the threshold — confirming the optimal decision is to predict cancer.

6.4.3 Computing Bayes Risk: The Cancer Example

For the cancer example, we can now compute the Bayes risk explicitly. First, applying the theorem above, the Bayes decision rule assigns:

  • $r^*(\text{miner}) = +1$ (cancer): because $L_{\text{fn}} \cdot 0.690 = 3.45 > L_{\text{fp}} \cdot 0.310 = 0.310$.
  • $r^*(\text{farmer}) = +1$ (cancer): because $L_{\text{fn}} \cdot 0.357 = 1.785 > L_{\text{fp}} \cdot 0.643 = 0.643$.
  • $r^*(\text{other}) = -1$ (no cancer): because $L_{\text{fn}} \cdot 0.036 = 0.180 < L_{\text{fp}} \cdot 0.964 = 0.964$.

The Bayes risk is then:

$$R^* = \sum_{x} \min(\Delta_{+1}(x), \Delta_{-1}(x)) \cdot P(X=x)$$ $$= \Delta_{+1}(\text{miner}) \cdot P(\text{miner}) + \Delta_{+1}(\text{farmer}) \cdot P(\text{farmer}) + \Delta_{-1}(\text{other}) \cdot P(\text{other})$$ $$= (0.310 \times 0.029) + (0.643 \times 0.140) + (0.036 \times 0.831) \approx 0.009 + 0.090 + 0.030 = 0.129.$$

So no matter how clever our classifier, if it is restricted to using occupation as its only feature, it can never achieve an expected loss below approximately 0.129 under our asymmetric loss function. This irreducible risk is a consequence of the overlap between the two class-conditional distributions.

Data Science Application · Risk Minimization as a Unifying Principle

The process of choosing $r$ to minimize $R(r)$ is called risk minimization, and it unifies a remarkable variety of machine learning algorithms. Least-squares regression minimizes squared-error risk. Logistic regression approximates cross-entropy risk. SVMs can be understood as minimizing hinge-loss risk with a regularization term. Every time you choose a loss function and train a model, you are doing risk minimization — whether or not your framework makes this explicit. We return to this theme when we discuss empirical risk minimization in Section 6.6.

6.5 Continuous Feature Spaces

So far we have worked with a discrete feature space — a finite set of occupations. But in most machine learning problems, features are continuous: the height of a person, the number of words in an email, the pixel values of an image. In moving from discrete to continuous features, the basic logic of Bayes classification remains unchanged, but the mathematical language shifts from probability mass functions and sums to probability density functions and integrals.

6.5.1 PDFs and Expected Values: A Brief Review

Definition · Probability Density Function and Expectation

A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is a probability density function (PDF) if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1$. For a random variable $X$ with PDF $f$, the probability that $X$ falls in an interval $[a, b]$ is $P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx$.

The expected value of a function $g(X)$ is $$\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\, f(x)\, dx.$$ In particular, $\mu = \mathbb{E}[X] = \int x\, f(x)\, dx$ is the mean and $\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2$ is the variance.

The class-conditional PDF for class $y$ is written $f_{X \mid Y=y}(x)$ — the density of the feature $X$ among all individuals with label $y$. The marginal density of $X$ is: $$f_X(x) = f_{X \mid Y=+1}(x)\, P(Y=+1) + f_{X \mid Y=-1}(x)\, P(Y=-1).$$ This is the continuous analogue of the law of total probability we used in Section 6.2.

6.5.2 The Continuous Bayes Classifier

With PDFs in hand, Bayes' theorem takes the following form for continuous features:

Theorem · Bayes' Theorem for Continuous Features

Let $X$ be a continuous feature with class-conditional PDFs $f_{X \mid Y=y}(x)$ and prior $P(Y=y)$. The posterior probability of class $y$ given the observed feature value $x$ is: $$P(Y = y \mid X = x) = \frac{f_{X \mid Y=y}(x)\, P(Y=y)}{f_X(x)}$$ where $f_X(x) = \sum_{y'} f_{X \mid Y=y'}(x)\, P(Y=y')$ is the marginal density of $X$.

Proof Sketch

This follows from the continuous version of Bayes' theorem applied to a mixed random vector $(X, Y)$ where $X$ is continuous and $Y$ is discrete. The joint density-probability is $p(x, y) = f_{X \mid Y=y}(x)\, P(Y=y)$. The conditional probability of $Y=y$ given $X=x$ is $p(x,y) / f_X(x)$, yielding the stated formula. (A complete measure-theoretic proof uses the Radon-Nikodym theorem.) □

The Bayes decision rule now becomes: predict $Y = +1$ at $x$ if $$L_{\text{fn}} \cdot f_{X \mid Y=+1}(x)\, P(Y=+1) > L_{\text{fp}} \cdot f_{X \mid Y=-1}(x)\, P(Y=-1).$$ Crucially, the $f_X(x)$ denominator cancels from both sides. This is why we never need to compute the marginal density $f_X(x)$ when doing Bayes classification — it is the same positive constant for all classes at a given $x$ and does not affect the comparison.

Figure 6.4. Top panel: Class-conditional PDFs $f_{X|Y=+1}(x)$ (red, $\mu_1=2$, $\sigma_1=1.2$) and $f_{X|Y=-1}(x)$ (blue, $\mu_{-1}=4.5$, $\sigma_{-1}=1.5$) before accounting for prior probabilities. Naive comparison of these curves would set the boundary near $x\approx 3.2$. Bottom panel: The same PDFs scaled by their prior probabilities ($P(Y=+1)=1/3$, $P(Y=-1)=2/3$). The intersection of the two scaled curves is the Bayes decision boundary (gold dashed line, $x \approx 2.8$): points to the left are classified as cancer, points to the right as no cancer. Scaling by the prior shifts the boundary toward the rarer class.

6.5.3 The Decision Boundary in 2D

In feature spaces of dimension $d > 1$, the Bayes decision boundary generalizes from a point (in 1D) to a $(d-1)$-dimensional surface. In 2D, it is a curve; in 3D, a surface; in general, a manifold separating the regions where $P(Y=+1 \mid \mathbf{x}) > P(Y=-1 \mid \mathbf{x})$ from where the reverse holds.

When the class-conditional distributions are multivariate Gaussians with the same covariance matrix but different means — a setting called linear discriminant analysis (LDA) — the Bayes decision boundary is a hyperplane. This is the simplest and most interpretable case, and it connects directly to the linear classifiers we studied earlier in the course.

Intuition · Why Equal Covariances Give a Linear Boundary

The Bayes decision boundary is defined by the equation $P(Y=+1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = P(Y=-1 \mid \mathbf{x})$. Substituting the Gaussian class-conditional densities and taking logarithms, the quadratic terms in $\mathbf{x}$ cancel when the covariance matrices are equal, leaving a linear equation in $\mathbf{x}$. If the covariances differ, the quadratic terms do not cancel, and the boundary becomes a quadratic surface — an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola in 2D. This is the setting studied in quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA).

Figure 6.6. Bayes decision boundary (gold dashed line) in a 2D feature space with two Gaussian classes having equal covariance matrices ($\sigma^2_1 = \sigma^2_2 = 0.81$, $\sigma^2_3 = \sigma^2_4 = 0.49$) and equal priors. Red points: class $Y=+1$ ($\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 = (1,1)^T$); blue points: class $Y=-1$ ($\boldsymbol{\mu}_2 = (3, 2.5)^T$). The background shading shows the posterior probability $P(Y=+1 \mid \mathbf{x})$: darker red = higher cancer posterior. The boundary is the level set where $P(Y=+1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = 0.5$, which is linear under equal-covariance Gaussians.
Data Science Application · Gaussian Naive Bayes and LDA

Two of the most widely used probabilistic classifiers are Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Both assume Gaussian class-conditional distributions. GNB additionally assumes that features are conditionally independent given the class label, making the joint class-conditional density a product of univariate Gaussians. LDA assumes equal covariance matrices, yielding a linear boundary. Despite their simplifying assumptions, both methods often perform remarkably well in practice — especially in high dimensions where learning a full covariance matrix is infeasible. We will study these methods in detail in the next chapter.

6.6 Empirical Risk Minimization

The Bayes decision rule is theoretically optimal: given the true joint distribution $P(X, Y)$, it achieves the lowest possible risk. The catch is that we rarely know the true distribution. In practice, we have a training set — a finite sample of $(X_i, Y_i)$ pairs drawn from the distribution — and we must estimate the distribution from this sample before we can apply Bayes' rule. This gap between theory and practice motivates the framework of empirical risk minimization.

6.6.1 When We Don't Know the True Distribution

Definition · Empirical Risk

Given a training set $\{(\mathbf{x}_1, y_1), \ldots, (\mathbf{x}_n, y_n)\}$ with $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i) \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} P(X, Y)$, the empirical risk of a decision rule $r$ is: $$\hat{R}(r) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n L(r(\mathbf{x}_i),\, y_i).$$ By the law of large numbers, $\hat{R}(r) \overset{p}{\to} R(r)$ as $n \to \infty$ for any fixed $r$. The empirical risk minimizer is $\hat{r} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{r \in \mathcal{H}} \hat{R}(r)$, where $\mathcal{H}$ is a hypothesis class (e.g., linear classifiers).

The distinction between $R(r)$ (the true, population-level risk) and $\hat{R}(r)$ (the empirical, training-set risk) is of central importance in learning theory. A classifier that achieves zero training error has $\hat{R}(r) = 0$, but its true risk $R(r)$ may be far from zero — this is the phenomenon of overfitting. Understanding when and why $\hat{R}(r) \approx R(r)$ is the subject of generalization theory, which we will develop in a later chapter.

Warning · Overfitting and the Empirical vs. True Risk

Minimizing $\hat{R}(r)$ over a very flexible hypothesis class can lead to $\hat{R}(r) \approx 0$ while $R(r)$ remains large. This happens because a sufficiently flexible classifier can memorize the training labels rather than learning the underlying distribution. The gap $R(r) - \hat{R}(r)$ is called the generalization gap, and controlling it requires either restricting the hypothesis class (regularization) or obtaining more data.

6.6.2 Risk Minimization as a Unifying Framework

The framework of risk minimization — choose a decision rule or model to minimize (empirical or true) risk — provides a single conceptual lens through which most classical machine learning algorithms can be understood.

AlgorithmLoss Function $L$Hypothesis Class $\mathcal{H}$Notes
PerceptronPerceptron loss: $\max(0, -y \langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle)$Linear classifiersOnline update; not exactly ERM
SVM (hard margin)0–1 loss (approximately)Max-margin linear classifiersSolved via quadratic program
SVM (soft margin)Hinge loss: $\max(0, 1 - y\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x}\rangle)$Linear classifiersRegularized ERM
Logistic RegressionLog loss: $\log(1 + e^{-y\langle \mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}\rangle})$Linear (in log-odds)Outputs calibrated probabilities
Bayes classifierAny $L(\hat{y}, y)$All measurable functionsMinimizes true risk; requires $P(X,Y)$
Least-squares regressionSquared error: $(y - \hat{y})^2$Linear functionsAlso used as classification proxy

Each row represents a different algorithm, but all are doing the same thing at a high level: choosing parameters of some function class to minimize an empirical estimate of a loss function. This perspective — ERM — is the foundation on which the statistical theory of learning is built. The word "empirical" in empirical risk minimization simply means that we are minimizing the risk as measured on the training data, rather than on the true (unknown) distribution.

Figure 6.7. Bayes risk $R^*$ (solid blue) as a function of the prior probability $P(Y=+1)$, for two Gaussian class-conditionals ($\mu_1=2$, $\sigma_1=1.2$; $\mu_{-1}=4.5$, $\sigma_{-1}=1.5$) under 0–1 loss. The gray dashed line shows the trivial classifier (always predict the majority class), which achieves risk $\min(P(Y=+1), P(Y=-1))$. The Bayes risk is always at or below the trivial baseline. At extreme priors (near 0 or 1), both strategies agree: it's almost always right to predict the dominant class. The gold vertical line marks the cancer example's prior ($P(Y=+1)=0.1$). At this prior, the Bayes classifier significantly outperforms the trivial one, because the class-conditional distributions are well-separated.
Intuition · What "Empirical" Means in Practice

The word "empirical" is modest: it acknowledges that we are working with the data we actually have, not the infinite-data ideal. In practice, empirical risk minimization works well when (1) we have enough data that $\hat{R}(r) \approx R(r)$, and (2) our hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is expressive enough to contain a good approximation of the Bayes-optimal $r^*$. Both conditions can fail — condition (1) fails when data is scarce (overfitting), and condition (2) fails when the hypothesis class is too rigid (underfitting). The bias-variance tradeoff, which we will study in depth later in the course, is precisely the tension between these two failure modes.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter developed the probabilistic foundations of classification. We began with the observation that real-world data often involves overlapping class distributions, making deterministic correct classification impossible. The right response to this uncertainty is not to ignore it but to model it: to learn probability distributions over classes and make decisions that account for both the probability of each outcome and its consequences.

The central computation of this chapter is the application of Bayes' theorem, which converts class-conditional probabilities (what we can estimate from labeled data) into posterior probabilities (what we need to make predictions). The Bayes decision rule — predict the class that minimizes expected loss, where loss encodes the relative badness of different error types — is the optimal classifier in the sense that no other classifier can achieve lower risk. The resulting framework, risk minimization, provides a unifying language for describing virtually every supervised learning algorithm.

Irreducible Error

When class-conditional distributions overlap, no classifier can achieve zero error. The Bayes risk $R^* = \mathbb{E}_X[1 - \max_y P(Y=y \mid X)]$ is the minimum achievable error rate. Striving for zero training error when $R^* > 0$ leads to overfitting.

Prior Probability

$P(Y=y)$ is the marginal class probability before observing features. The prior reflects the base rate of each class in the population. Ignoring the prior leads to the base rate fallacy — e.g., concluding a rare disease is likely from a high class-conditional hit rate alone.

Class-Conditional Probability

$P(X=x \mid Y=y)$ or $f_{X|Y=y}(x)$ is the distribution of feature $x$ within class $y$. This is what supervised training data directly estimates. It answers: "Among cancer patients, how common is each occupation?"

Posterior Probability

$P(Y=y \mid X=x) \propto P(X=x \mid Y=y)\, P(Y=y)$ is the key quantity for classification, obtained via Bayes' theorem. It answers: "Given that a person has this occupation, how likely is cancer?" This is the quantity the classifier must maximize.

Loss Function

$L(\hat{y}, y) \geq 0$ with $L(y,y)=0$ quantifies the cost of predicting $\hat{y}$ when the truth is $y$. Asymmetric losses ($L_{\text{fn}} \neq L_{\text{fp}}$) are appropriate when false positives and negatives have different consequences — medical diagnosis, fraud detection, spam filtering.

Risk = Expected Loss

$R(r) = \mathbb{E}[L(r(X), Y)]$ is the expected cost of decision rule $r$ over the data distribution. Memorize this: risk is always expected loss. Every classical ML algorithm minimizes some form of risk (possibly empirical, possibly regularized).

Bayes Decision Rule

$r^*(x) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y'} \sum_y L(y', y)\, P(Y=y \mid x)$. Under 0–1 loss this reduces to: predict the class with the highest posterior. Under asymmetric loss, the threshold shifts: predict $+1$ iff $L_{\text{fn}} P(Y=+1 \mid x) > L_{\text{fp}} P(Y=-1 \mid x)$.

Bayes Risk

$R^* = R(r^*)$ is the minimum achievable risk under any decision rule. It is a property of the joint distribution $P(X,Y)$ and the loss function — not of any particular algorithm. Computing $R^*$ sets the performance benchmark for a given classification problem.

Marginal Density Cancels

In computing the Bayes decision rule, $f_X(x)$ or $P(X=x)$ appears in both posteriors' denominators and cancels. We never need to compute the marginal distribution of $X$ to classify. This simplification is practically important — estimating $f_X(x)$ in high dimensions is hard.

Empirical Risk Minimization

$\hat{R}(r) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i L(r(\mathbf{x}_i), y_i) \overset{p}{\to} R(r)$. Since the true distribution is unknown, we minimize training risk as a proxy. The gap $R(r) - \hat{R}(r)$ is the generalization gap; controlling it is the central problem of learning theory, and motivates regularization.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 · Bayes' Theorem Application
Email Spam Detection with Asymmetric Costs

A spam filter uses the presence of the word "free" as a single feature. In the training data, 40% of emails are spam. Among spam emails, 80% contain "free"; among legitimate emails, 5% contain "free."

  1. Derivation: Compute $P(X=\text{"free"})$, $P(\text{spam} \mid X=\text{"free"})$, and $P(\text{spam} \mid X=\text{no "free"})$ using Bayes' theorem. Show all steps.
  2. Computation: Using 0–1 loss, what should the spam filter predict for emails containing "free"? For emails not containing "free"? Compute the Bayes risk under 0–1 loss.
  3. Asymmetric loss: Now suppose filtering a legitimate email as spam has loss $L_{\text{fp}} = 10$, while letting spam through has loss $L_{\text{fn}} = 1$. Recompute the optimal decision for emails containing "free." Qualitatively explain why the threshold shifted.
  4. Extension: In a production email system, the prior $P(\text{spam})$ varies over time as spam campaigns come and go. Explain how a well-designed spam filter should update its classifier as the prior shifts, without retraining on new labeled data.
Exercise 6.2 · Loss Functions and Optimal Thresholds
Deriving the Decision Threshold for General Asymmetric Loss

Consider a binary classifier with posteriors $p_+ = P(Y=+1 \mid X=x)$ and $p_- = 1 - p_+$, and an asymmetric loss with false-positive loss $L_{\text{fp}} > 0$ and false-negative loss $L_{\text{fn}} > 0$.

  1. Derivation: Starting from the Bayes decision rule, derive the critical posterior threshold $p^*$ such that we predict $+1$ if and only if $p_+ > p^*$. Express $p^*$ in terms of $L_{\text{fp}}$ and $L_{\text{fn}}$.
  2. Computation: Compute $p^*$ for the following scenarios: (i) 0–1 loss, (ii) $L_{\text{fn}} = 3L_{\text{fp}}$, (iii) $L_{\text{fn}} = 10L_{\text{fp}}$. What happens to the threshold as $L_{\text{fn}} / L_{\text{fp}} \to \infty$?
  3. Interpretation: A financial fraud detection system catches 90% of fraudulent transactions but also flags 15% of legitimate ones. Describe how you would use the loss ratio $L_{\text{fn}} / L_{\text{fp}}$ to decide whether this is an acceptable trade-off. What information would you need from the business to determine the loss ratio?
  4. Extension: Suppose we have a multi-class problem with $K > 2$ classes and an arbitrary $K \times K$ loss matrix $L$ with $L_{ii} = 0$. Write down the generalization of the Bayes decision rule. Does it still reduce to "predict the highest-posterior class" under 0–1 loss? Prove your answer.
Exercise 6.3 · Continuous Bayes Classifier
Gaussian Class-Conditionals and the Decision Boundary

Suppose $X \mid Y=+1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_+, \sigma^2)$ and $X \mid Y=-1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_-, \sigma^2)$ with a common variance $\sigma^2$, and prior $P(Y=+1) = \pi$.

  1. Derivation: Write out the posterior $P(Y=+1 \mid X=x)$ explicitly. Show that $\log \frac{P(Y=+1 \mid X=x)}{P(Y=-1 \mid X=x)}$ is a linear function of $x$, and identify the slope and intercept in terms of $\mu_+$, $\mu_-$, $\sigma^2$, and $\pi$.
  2. Computation: For $\mu_+ = 2$, $\mu_- = 5$, $\sigma = 1.5$, $\pi = 0.3$, find the exact Bayes decision boundary $x^*$ under 0–1 loss. (Solve analytically — no numerical methods needed.)
  3. Interpretation: How does the boundary $x^*$ move as the prior $\pi$ increases from 0 to 1? Interpret this geometrically: in which direction does $x^*$ move, and why does this make intuitive sense?
  4. Data science connection: This model (Gaussian class-conditionals, equal variance) is precisely Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The decision boundary you derived in (a) is a linear classifier. Compare its form to the SVM classifier studied earlier in the course. In what sense is LDA a "probabilistic SVM"? In what sense are they fundamentally different?
Exercise 6.4 · Bayes Risk and Irreducible Error
Computing and Interpreting the Performance Floor

Consider a binary classification problem where $P(Y=+1) = \pi$ and the two class-conditional distributions are $X \mid Y=+1 \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 2)$ and $X \mid Y=-1 \sim \text{Uniform}(1, 3)$.

  1. Derivation: Compute the Bayes decision boundary (or boundaries) under 0–1 loss for $\pi = 0.5$. Be careful about the three regions: $[0,1)$, $[1,2]$, $(2,3]$. In each region, determine which class has higher posterior and what the optimal prediction is.
  2. Computation: Compute the Bayes risk $R^*$ under 0–1 loss for $\pi = 0.5$. Then compute $R^*$ for $\pi = 0.2$ and $\pi = 0.8$. Interpret the trend.
  3. Interpretation: Explain in words why the Bayes risk is non-zero for $\pi = 0.5$ in this example. What property of the data-generating process causes the irreducible error? Could you eliminate it by collecting more training data?
  4. Extension: Suppose a practitioner reports that their classifier achieves 88% accuracy on a held-out test set for this problem (with $\pi=0.5$). Is this good performance? Justify your answer quantitatively using the Bayes risk you computed.
Exercise 6.5 · Empirical Risk Minimization
From Population Risk to Training Risk in Text Classification

You are building a sentiment classifier (positive/negative) for product reviews, using a training set of $n = 1000$ labeled reviews and a test set of $500$ reviews. You train a linear classifier $r_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}) = \text{sign}(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x})$ by minimizing the empirical 0–1 risk (approximately, via a surrogate loss).

  1. Derivation: Define the empirical risk $\hat{R}(r_{\mathbf{w}})$ and the true risk $R(r_{\mathbf{w}})$ formally for this problem. State the law of large numbers result that justifies using $\hat{R}$ as a proxy for $R$. What assumption about the training data is required for this result to hold?
  2. Computation: Your classifier achieves 95% training accuracy and 82% test accuracy. Compute $\hat{R}$ and estimate $R$ from the test set. What is the generalization gap? Is this a well-fitted model, an overfitted model, or an underfitted model? Justify.
  3. Interpretation: A colleague suggests adding a regularization term to the empirical risk: $\hat{R}_\lambda(r_{\mathbf{w}}) = \hat{R}(r_{\mathbf{w}}) + \lambda \|\mathbf{w}\|^2$. Explain from the perspective of the bias-variance tradeoff what effect increasing $\lambda$ will have on training accuracy, test accuracy, and the generalization gap.
  4. Extension: The product review platform later discovers that the test set was collected two years after the training set, and the distribution of review language has shifted (e.g., new slang, new products). Which of the conditions required for $\hat{R} \approx R$ is violated? How does this affect the validity of your empirical risk estimate? What practical steps could address this issue?
